home.headline:
One technique.
A whole toolkit.
home.intro: MiniShield flattens control flow — one hardening technique among many. The Volume 1 capstone showed the plugin is a framework that hosts techniques as named passes. This crash course fills it: control-flow integrity, stack canaries, OLLVM-style obfuscation, position independence, and the fuzzing that proves each one still behaves.

aside.label: Roadmap
aside.text: Volume 3 is a crash course, not a second implementation: each technique gets its threat, its mechanism, concrete LLVM IR, and its cost. The OLLVM family you implement in the same plugin; CFI, canaries, and PIE are read and verified with the toolchain.

lessons.title: The code-hardening landscape
lessons.summary: Place control-flow flattening in the threat model, name the hardening families this volume covers, and set the standard for claiming a hardening technique works.
lessons.takeaway: Flattening is one family — obfuscation. Each technique answers a different threat at a different cost, and obfuscation is the only family whose value the final optimizer can remove.

blocks.text: So far MiniShield has implemented one code-hardening technique: control-flow flattening, which rewrites the control flow of an accepted function through a state-machine dispatcher. The final lesson of Volume 1 zoomed out from there: the plugin’s seams — the named-pass registry, per-technique eligibility guard, shared CFG analysis, and the differential and stats harness — are technique-agnostic, so each hardening technique becomes one more named pass. This volume fills that framework with concrete techniques, organized by the threat each one answers rather than by the seam it plugs into. Every chapter follows the same shape: the threat, the mechanism, concrete LLVM IR from the 23.1.5 toolchain, an exercise, and the cost.
Threats and the families that answer them

rows: Reads or patches the program’s logic
Control-flow flattening (Volume 2) · bogus control flow · string encryption · subroutine splitting
Redirects control through a corrupted indirect call, vtable pointer, or function pointer
Corrupts the saved return address and hijacks a function’s return
Predicts where code sits in memory and defeats ASLR
Finds the memory bugs the rest assume are absent
Sanitizers — used in this volume’s tests and fuzzing, not shipped

blocks.text: The table is a division of labor, not a ranking. CFI stops a corrupted vtable pointer from dispatching to the wrong type, but it does nothing against an attacker who simply reads the binary to find the hole. Obfuscation makes that reading harder, but it does not make a buffer overflow safe. A hardening program layers the families so that no single compromise gives the attacker what they need; this volume teaches each layer separately so you can see where the seams are.
Where MiniShield’s flattening sits

Flattening is the obfuscation family’s member in this book. It raises the cost of understanding and changing control flow, and it pays for that at runtime — a state slot, a load, a switch, and the straight-line optimizations the dispatcher destroys — and at the end of the pipeline: a sufficiently aggressive final optimizer can simplify the state machine back toward the original program, and Volume 2’s exit evidence ends with exactly that observation. Obfuscation has a quality problem the other families do not: its value is what survives optimization, not what the pass emits. Every chapter in this volume returns to that question for its technique.
How this volume works

items: Each technique gets the same shape: the threat it answers, the mechanism, concrete LLVM IR generated and verified with the isolated LLVM 23.1.5 teaching references, a hands-on exercise, and the cost and limits.

The OLLVM family — bogus control flow, string encryption, subroutine splitting — you implement as new passes in the MiniShield plugin, using the capstone recipe (register, guard, builder, orchestrator, fixtures), and you prove each one preserves behavior with the differential-testing method from the Volume 2 testing chapters.
CFI, stack canaries, and position independence are taught by reading and verifying what clang already generates — a from-scratch CFI pass is beyond crash-course scope.
The final lesson fuzzes one of your own passes, because a differential test over a fixed seed covers less than a fuzzer over the same property.

blocks.text: Two terms before the chapters. A threat model is the explicit statement of which attacker you are defending against and what success means for them. Hardening quality is judged on what that attacker can still do after the technique, at what cost to legitimate users — structural observations like “the block count doubled” or “a canary is present” are not quality claims by themselves.

Checkpoint: MiniShield’s flattening raises the cost of reverse engineering. Of the threats in the table, which does it actually answer, which does it leave open, and why is its failure mode different from the failure modes of CFI and canaries?

items: It answers the first row — reading or patching the program’s logic: the flattened CFG hides the control structure behind a dispatcher and a state slot, so understanding or modifying behavior requires modeling the state machine.

It leaves the other rows open: a corrupted indirect call or vtable pointer (the CFI threat), a corrupted return address (the canary threat), and the memory bugs themselves all still work against the flattened program, because flattening rearranges control flow instead of changing what the program executes or where its data lives.

Its failure mode is optimization, not bypass: the final optimizer can prove the state machine’s behavior and simplify it back toward the original CFG (the Volume 2 exit evidence reduces the whole dispatcher to one select), so the shipped artifact can be structurally unhardened. CFI checks and canaries change what the program does at runtime, so they survive optimization; obfuscation’s quality must be judged on the final artifact, not on the pass output.

lessons.title: The indirect call check
lessons.summary: Forward CFI guards indirect calls: read the llvm.type.test + llvm.ubsantrap IR that clang 23.1.5 emits under -fsanitize=cfi-icall -flto, understand why the guard exists only where LTO cannot resolve the target, and verify at runtime that a wrong-type call aborts with SIGILL.
lessons.takeaway: CFI-ICALL is a type test on the callee pointer, inserted by LTO only where the target is genuinely unknown: it aborts wrong-type targets with SIGILL and says nothing about a wrong function of the right type.

blocks.text: Forward CFI (CFI-ICALL) answers the first concrete threat in the landscape: an attacker overwrites a function pointer — via a buffer overflow, a corrupted pointer table, a data race — and the program calls whatever the pointer now says. The pointer is data, and the call site trusts it unconditionally. Forward CFI inserts a guard before every indirect call: verify that the target has the expected function type before dispatching. In LLVM 23.1.5 the guard is the `llvm.type.test` intrinsic paired with `llvm.ubsantrap`, not the legacy `llvm.cfi_icheck` intrinsic that older material describes.
The check in IR

Minimal case: a program obtains a function pointer from an extern function — outside this translation unit, so the compiler can never know where it points. This is what clang 23.1.5 emits with `-fsanitize=cfi-icall -flto -O2` (trimmed from the real capture; `opt -passes=verify` accepts it):

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare ptr @lookup(i32)

declare i1 @llvm.type.test(ptr, metadata)
declare void @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 immarg)

define i32 @run_op(i32 %id, i32 %x) {
  %fp = tail call ptr @lookup(i32 %id)
  %ok = tail call i1 @llvm.type.test(ptr %fp, metadata !"_ZTSFiiE")
  br i1 %ok, label %do_call, label %trap

trap:
  tail call void @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 2)
  unreachable

do_call:
  %r = tail call i32 %fp(i32 %x)
  ret i32 %r
}

Read it top to bottom. `%fp` is the attacker-controlled pointer: it comes from `lookup`, which lives in another translation unit, so even full LTO cannot resolve it. `%ok` is the guard: `llvm.type.test` asks whether the memory at `%fp` carries a CFI type descriptor matching `_ZTSFiiE` — the mangled type-info name of the function type `int(int)`. The descriptor is attached by the compiler to every function compiled with CFI; a target without one, or with a different one, fails the test. The branch then goes to `do_call`, where the real indirect call happens, or to `trap`, where `llvm.ubsantrap` lowers to an undefined instruction and the process dies with SIGILL (exit 132).

Two things this is not. First, it is not an address check: nothing compares `%fp` against a list of allowed addresses, so a target of the right type but the wrong function still passes. Second, the guard exists only where the target is unknown. Without the flag, the same source compiles to an unconditional indirect call:

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare ptr @lookup(i32)

define i32 @run_op(i32 %id, i32 %x) {
  %fp = tail call ptr @lookup(i32 %id)
  %r = tail call i32 %fp(i32 %x)
  ret i32 %r
}
Where LTO can see the target, the check changes shape

CFI-ICALL is an LTO feature — the flag refuses to work without `-flto`. LTO's job is to resolve indirect calls, so most guards the front end would emit disappear at link time: when the target is provably unique the call is devirtualized or inlined, and there is nothing to guard. Where the target set is small but not fully resolvable, the generic type test degenerates into a comparison against known addresses. In the single-translation-unit demo below, LTO rewrote the guard as:

The parsed address is compared against `0x201830` — the address of `op_right`, the only target of the right type — and a mismatch jumps to the `ud1` trap. Note that `op_right` itself is now a one-instruction thunk that jumps to `op_right.cfi`, the body LTO rebuilt with its CFI type descriptor attached. The shape to take away: the guard appears exactly where the pointer is genuinely unknown at link time — external, data-dependent, attacker-writable — in whatever form is cheapest there.
Proof at runtime

The demo program reads a pointer address from standard input and calls through it; a `self` flag prints the addresses of the two candidate targets (a legal `int(int)` function and a wrong-type `int()` function). It is linked with `-no-pie` so the printed addresses are stable across runs — under ASLR each launch would print different ones (the PIE chapter returns to exactly that point).

$ clang-23 -fsanitize=cfi-icall -flto -O2 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld cfi_pipe.c -o cfi_pipe
$ clang-23 -flto -O2 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld cfi_pipe.c -o cfi_pipe_nocfi
$ ./cfi_pipe self
0x201830 0x201790
$ echo 0x201830 | ./cfi_pipe
result -> 42
$ echo 0x201790 | ./cfi_pipe
Illegal instruction (core dumped)
$ ./cfi_pipe_nocfi self
0x201778 0x201780
$ echo 0x201780 | ./cfi_pipe_nocfi
result -> 99

The legal target dispatches and returns 42. The wrong-type target dies with an illegal instruction — that is the CFI trap, a hard abort, not a report. And in the binary built without CFI, the same wrong-type input does not crash at all: the call goes through, `op_wrong` returns 99, and the program prints it as a normal result. That silent success is the threat CFI removes — a corrupted pointer that lands on a function with a matching calling convention but the wrong behavior; the only observable difference is the wrong answer. CFI turns that into a visible abort.

items: `-fsanitize=cfi-icall` works only with `-flto`, and every object in the link must be CFI-instrumented: a non-CFI target has no type descriptor to match, so even a legal call aborts.

LTO removes every guard whose target it can resolve and folds the rest to the cheapest correct form; a program whose indirect calls all have known targets contains no CFI checks at all, and that is not a misconfiguration.
The check is on the target's type, not its address: a wrong function of the matching signature is still a legal target.
`llvm.ubsantrap` lowers to an undefined instruction (SIGILL, exit 132), not a message; without a debugger the failure looks like a random illegal instruction, not a CFI violation.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: In the demo the wrong-type target aborts and the legal target completes. (a) What does the guard test, and where does the value it matches come from? (b) Why does the guard appear in this program at all? (c) Why is the no-CFI run a more dangerous failure than the CFI run?

items: (a) It tests the target's function-type descriptor: `llvm.type.test` compares what the compiler attached to each CFI-compiled function definition against `_ZTSFiiE`, the mangled type-info name of the function type `int(int)`. It is not an address — a wrong function of the right type still passes.

(b) Because the callee pointer is genuinely unknown at link time: in the minimal module it comes from the extern `lookup`, and in the demo it is parsed from standard input at runtime. LTO can only remove or fold the guard when it can resolve the target, and it cannot here.

(c) Without CFI the wrong-type call silently succeeds — it prints `result -> 99` and exits 0: the corruption achieved its goal and nobody knows. With CFI the process aborts with SIGILL: the hijack is blocked and visible. A check that fails silently is worse than no check, because it hides the attack; CFI's value is in making the failure a crash.

lessons.title: The vtable check
lessons.summary: Backward CFI guards virtual calls: read the vtable-pointer llvm.type.test that clang++ 23.1.5 emits under -fsanitize=cfi-vcall, understand which corruptions it catches and which it misses, and verify at runtime that a wrong-class vtable aborts while a derived-class vtable passes.
lessons.takeaway: CFI-VCALL tests the vtable pointer against the static base-class descriptor before dispatch: it catches an object with the wrong class's vtable, not a legitimate vtable with corrupted slots.

blocks.text: CFI-ICALL guards the callee pointer. The more common C++ threat is one level up: the object's vtable pointer. A corrupted vptr — a type-confusion write, a buffer overflow that reaches the first word of an object, a stale pointer into a reused allocation — makes `b->apply(x)` dispatch to a completely unrelated class. CFI-VCALL inserts a guard before every virtual call: the vtable pointer must point into the type-info hierarchy of the call site's static base class.
The check is on the vtable pointer

Captured with clang++ 23.1.5 and `-fsanitize=cfi-vcall -fvisibility=hidden -flto -O2` (hidden visibility is required; the flag is refused without it). Trimmed from the real capture, `opt -passes=verify` accepts it:

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare i1 @llvm.type.test(ptr, metadata)
declare void @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 immarg)

define i32 @run_op(i64 %obj, i32 %x) {
  %objptr = inttoptr i64 %obj to ptr
  %vtable = load ptr, ptr %objptr, align 8
  %ok = call i1 @llvm.type.test(ptr %vtable, metadata !"_ZTS4Base")
  br i1 %ok, label %do_call, label %trap

trap:
  call void @llvm.ubsantrap(i8 2)
  unreachable

do_call:
  %slot = load ptr, ptr %vtable, align 8
  %r = call i32 %slot(ptr %objptr, i32 %x)
  ret i32 %r
}

Two differences from the ICALL guard. The pointer under test is not a function address but the vtable pointer loaded from the object's first word — `%vtable = load ptr, ptr %objptr`. And the descriptor is not a function-type name but the mangled class name of the call site's static type: `_ZTS4Base` is the type-info name of `Base`. `llvm.type.test` succeeds when the vtable belongs to `Base` or to a class derived from it — C++'s dynamic-type rule, enforced at every dispatch. If it passes, dispatch proceeds exactly as usual: load slot 0 of the vtable and call through it.

Together the pair covers the two indirect dispatches a C++ program performs: ICALL tests a function pointer against the function's type; VCALL tests a vtable pointer against the class's type. Same intrinsic, same trap, different operand and different descriptor.
Proof at runtime

$ clang++-23 -fsanitize=cfi-vcall -fvisibility=hidden -flto -O2 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld vcall_pipe.cpp -o vcall_pipe
$ ./vcall_pipe self
0x203df8 0x203e00
$ echo 0x203df8 | ./vcall_pipe
result -> 42
$ echo 0x203e00 | ./vcall_pipe
Illegal instruction (core dumped)

The program prints the addresses of two static objects — a `Derived` (which derives from `Base`) and an `Evil` (which does not) — and then dispatches through the address read from standard input. `Derived` passes: its vtable is in `Base`'s hierarchy, and the call returns 42. `Evil` fails: it does not derive from `Base`, so its vtable is not registered under `Base`'s type-info, and the type test aborts the process before any vtable slot is loaded.

The boundary matters. CFI-VCALL catches the vtable being the wrong class, not the right class with the wrong slots: an attacker who overwrites slot 0 of a legitimate `Derived` vtable to point at their own function still passes the check, because the vtable pointer is in the right hierarchy, and the hijack goes through. That is the same type-versus-address distinction as the previous lesson, one level up.

items: `-fsanitize=cfi-vcall` requires `-fvisibility=hidden`; the compiler rejects the flag without it.
The check is on the vtable pointer (the object's first word), not on the method pointer loaded from the vtable: a corrupted slot in a legitimate class's vtable is not caught.
Like CFI-ICALL this is an LTO feature: calls LTO can devirtualize — the common case once it has proved the dynamic type — carry no guard at all.

The descriptor is the static type at the call site (here `Base`); a call through a pointer of a more-derived type is checked against that more-derived type, so the check composes up the derivation chain.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: In the demo the `Derived` dispatch succeeds and the `Evil` dispatch aborts. (a) Which pointer does the guard test, and against which descriptor? (b) Why does clang require `-fvisibility=hidden` for this flag? (c) What corruption of a legitimate vtable would this check not stop?

items: (a) The vtable pointer loaded from the object's first word, tested against `_ZTS4Base` — the type-info name of the call site's static base class — not against the address of the method that will be called.

(b) The guard compares the object's vtable pointer against a local, compile-time-known vtable/type-info address. With default-visibility type-info symbols the dynamic linker can interpose a different copy from another shared object, and the check would silently test against the wrong address; `-fvisibility=hidden` pins the type-info symbols to the local copies, which is why clang accepts the flag only with it.

(c) A corrupted slot inside a legitimate vtable: overwrite slot 0 of a real `Derived` vtable to point at attacker code and the vtable pointer still points into the right hierarchy, the check passes, and the dispatch is hijacked. CFI-VCALL verifies which class an object claims to be, not what that class's vtable points to.

lessons.title: The stack canary check
lessons.summary: Read the stack canary the way clang 23.1.5 actually emits it: the sspstrong attribute in the IR, the TLS plant/compare/abort machinery in the machine code, which functions each -fstack-protector mode protects, and the runtime proof that the same overflow is a silent hijack without the canary and a visible abort with it.
lessons.takeaway: A stack canary is a per-process random value planted between the buffer and the saved return address and checked at function exit: it turns the classic return-address hijack into a visible abort, but it only guards what its own frame guards — not globals, not the heap, not unprotected functions, and not a leaked guard.

blocks.text: Stack canaries answer the control-data row of the threat table: an attacker overwrites the saved return address of a function — the classic buffer overflow — and the function returns into their code instead of its caller. The canary is a random value planted in the frame between the vulnerable buffer and the saved return address, and compared on the way out: if the overflow reached the return address, it crossed the canary, and the comparison aborts the process before the corrupted return executes. Unlike CFI, the canary changes what data the frame holds rather than what the control flow may target.
One thing to hold in mind while reading this chapter: you will not find the canary in the IR. This is what clang 23.1.5 actually leaves behind, and where the check really lives.
The canary is not in the IR

The vulnerable function is `process`, an unchecked copy of an attacker-controlled length into a 16-byte buffer. Compiled with `-fstack-protector-strong -O0`, the module is (attribute bundle trimmed; `opt -passes=verify` accepts it):

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare i64 @strlen(ptr noundef)
declare void @llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64(ptr noalias writeonly, ptr noalias readonly, i64, i1 immarg)

; clang 23.1.5, -fstack-protector-strong -O0; attribute bundle trimmed
define dso_local i32 @process(ptr noundef %line) #0 {
  %2 = alloca ptr, align 8
  %3 = alloca [16 x i8], align 16
  %4 = alloca i32, align 4
  store ptr %line, ptr %2, align 8
  store i32 0, ptr %4, align 4
  %5 = getelementptr inbounds [16 x i8], ptr %3, i64 0, i64 0
  %6 = load ptr, ptr %2, align 8
  %8 = call i64 @strlen(ptr noundef %6)
  call void @llvm.memcpy.p0.p0.i64(ptr align 16 %5, ptr align 1 %6, i64 %8, i1 false)
  %9 = load i32, ptr %4, align 4
  %10 = add nsw i32 %9, 1
  ret i32 %10
}

attributes #0 = { sspstrong "stack-protector-buffer-size"="8" }

Grep this module for a canary and you find nothing: no intrinsic, no call, no store. The entire trace of the protection in the IR is `sspstrong` in the function's attribute bundle, alongside the `"stack-protector-buffer-size"` value. The default build of the same source is identical except that `sspstrong` is absent from the bundle — no other IR byte changes. (LLVM 23 does define an `llvm.stackprotector` intrinsic in its Intrinsics.td — it "writes the stack guard to the correct place on the stack frame" — but this C pipeline never emits it; the guard is materialized directly in machine code.) The backend, reading the attribute, is what generates the canary.
The machine code where the canary lives

This is the backend's output for the same function (`-fstack-protector-strong -O0`; `.cfi` directives omitted). The frame is `subq $64`: the buffer at `-32(%rbp)`, the canary slot at `-8(%rbp)`, the saved return address at `+8(%rbp)`:

process:
	pushq	%rbp
	movq	%rsp, %rbp
	subq	$64, %rsp
	movq	%fs:40, %rax
	movq	%rax, -8(%rbp)
	movq	%rdi, -40(%rbp)
	movl	$0, -44(%rbp)
	movq	-40(%rbp), %rdi
	movq	%rdi, -56(%rbp)
	callq	strlen@PLT
	movq	-56(%rbp), %rsi
	movq	%rax, %rdx
	leaq	-32(%rbp), %rdi
	callq	memcpy@PLT
	movl	-44(%rbp), %eax
	incl	%eax
	movl	%eax, -48(%rbp)
	movq	%fs:40, %rax
	movq	-8(%rbp), %rcx
	cmpq	%rcx, %rax
	jne	.LBB1_2
	movl	-48(%rbp), %eax
	addq	$64, %rsp
	popq	%rbp
	retq
.LBB1_2:
	callq	__stack_chk_fail@PLT

Read it in three beats. Entry: `movq %fs:40, %rax` loads the guard from per-process TLS, and `movq %rax, -8(%rbp)` plants the copy in the frame between the buffer and the return address — exactly the placement the `--help` text promises: the guard "must be positioned in the stack frame such that a buffer overflow from a vulnerable variable will overwrite the guard value before overwriting the function's return address." Exit: the guard is reloaded from TLS, compared with the planted copy, and a mismatch jumps to `callq __stack_chk_fail@PLT`, which aborts the process. Note the value's origin: one random number in TLS per process — the same value is planted in every protected frame, not one per frame.
Which functions get a canary
The mode flag selects which frames the backend protects. Three function shapes in one TU, compiled four ways (clang 23.1.5, `-O0`):

rows: takes the address of a local

blocks.text: The `--help` text states the heuristics: plain mode protects functions with char arrays larger than 8 bytes; strong adds arrays of any type, `alloca` calls, and taking the address of a local variable; `-all` protects every function. Note that `f_ptr` trips strong because of `memcpy(&c, ...)` — the address of a local — not because of its pointer parameter. And the default of this toolchain is no canaries at all: many distributions' compilers turn on `-fstack-protector-strong` by default, but the conda clang here does not, which is why every command in this lesson spells the flag out.
Proof at runtime

The demo builds a 56-byte payload in `main` — 24 bytes of padding, then the address of `sink` (a function that prints and exits) repeated four times — and passes it to `process` with its explicit length, so no NUL byte in the address can truncate the copy. The spray covers whichever 8-byte slot the saved return address lands in. As in the CFI chapter, `-no-pie` keeps the printed addresses stable across runs.

$ clang-23 -O0 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld canary_pipe.c -o canary
$ clang-23 -fstack-protector-strong -O0 -no-pie -fuse-ld=lld canary_pipe.c -o canary_strong
$ ./canary self
0x201810
$ echo 0x201810 | ./canary
HACKED: process returned into sink
$ echo 0x201810 | ./canary_strong
*** stack smashing detected ***: terminated
Aborted (core dumped)

Without the canary, the overflow rewrites the saved return address to `sink`: the program prints `HACKED` and the hijack has succeeded silently — exit 0, no error of any kind. With the canary, the same overflow smashes the guard at `-8(%rbp)` on its way to the return address; the exit check finds the mismatch and aborts before the corrupted return executes — exit 134 (SIGABRT), "stack smashing detected." Same overflow, same payload: one build lets the attack land, the other turns it into a crash. That is the canary's value proposition, and it is the same shape as CFI's — a silent compromise becomes a visible abort — aimed at control data instead of control-flow targets.
What the canary does not stop

items: Global or heap function pointers: the canary guards the saved return address of one frame. It says nothing about a corrupted pointer in `.data` or on the heap, which never touches the frame.
Functions the heuristic did not protect: `f_math` above carries no guard and no check, so an overflow in an unprotected frame is invisible to the canary.
Corrupted locals used before the return: if an overflow stops short of the guard slot — say, clobbering a vtable pointer in a local object — the damage is done while the canary is still intact.
A known guard: the value is one random number per process, in TLS. An attacker who can read memory can read the canary and write it back around the overflow.

Buffers the final optimizer erases: at `-O2`, `process` becomes `movl $1, %eax; retq` — the buffer, the overflow, and the canary all disappear together, because the protection only survives as long as the state it protects does.

blocks.text: The cost is small and local: one TLS load at entry, one store, one TLS load plus one compare at exit, per protected function, plus a cold branch to the abort. It is a runtime check in the same class as the CFI trap, not a compile-time property — and like the CFI trap, its whole value is in aborting loudly rather than continuing wrong.

items: The canary lives in machine code, not IR: grepping the `.ll` for a guard finds nothing. The evidence is the `sspstrong` attribute in the bundle and the `%fs:` load in the asm.
The guard is per-process, not per-frame: one TLS value for the whole address space. Leaking that one value defeats every canary in the process.
The demo is `-O0` on purpose: at `-O2` the optimizer erases the vulnerable buffer and the protection disappears with the state it protects.
Partial corruption of the guard slot is enough to trip the check: the compare covers all 8 bytes, so any overlap of the overflow with the guard aborts.
This toolchain's default is no canaries; the flag is explicit in every command in this lesson.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: In the demo the no-canary build reaches `sink` and the canary build aborts. (a) Where does the guard value come from, and where in the frame is it planted? (b) What is the only trace of the protection in the IR, and why does that make the canary invisible to an IR-only reader? (c) Name one overflow that still succeeds against the canary build, and say why the canary cannot see it.

items: (a) The guard is a per-process value in TLS (`movq %fs:40, %rax` — the same number for every frame in the process). Entry stores a copy in the frame at `-8(%rbp)`, between the vulnerable buffer at `-32(%rbp)` and the saved return address at `+8(%rbp)`, so an overflow from the buffer must cross the guard to reach the return address.

(b) `sspstrong` in the function's attribute bundle (with `"stack-protector-buffer-size"`). The frontend only records which frames are eligible; the backend materializes the load/store/compare from that attribute, so an IR-only reader sees no canary instructions at all — the protection is a property of the generated machine code, not of the IR.

(c) For example, overwriting a global function pointer: the canary guards only the saved return address of protected frames. A corrupted dispatch pointer in `.data` never touches any frame's guard, the program dispatches through it, and no canary is ever consulted — the check exists only at the exit of instrumented functions, and only for their own return path.

lessons.title: Bogus control flow
lessons.summary: OLLVM's bogus control flow transform as a learner pass: an opaque-predicate gate on every conditional branch, dead redundant blocks on the false side, the -O0 differential proof, and the -O2 dissolution — constant seeds fold, runtime seeds die by dead-store elimination, and only opaque side effects survive, hoisted into a single sink.
lessons.takeaway: Bogus control flow adds dead structure guarded by a predicate the optimizer cannot prove. Its quality is a property of the final artifact, not of the pass output: at -O2 the gates fold or the dead blocks are emptied, and what survives of the transform is only what the optimizer is not allowed to delete — a side effect it cannot see.

blocks.text: This part treats three OLLVM-family obfuscations as MiniShield passes, added one at a time with the Volume 1 capstone recipe: register the name in `lib/Plugin.cpp`, encode the support contract in a guard, write the builder, orchestrate eligibility, build, verify, and close with a fixture pair whose before and after pass `opt -passes=verify` and run identically. OLLVM is the 2015 project that collected these transforms for LLVM: each changes the program's structure without changing its behavior, on the assumption that a static reader — a person or an analysis tool — spends time on the added structure. That assumption is the one the landscape lesson put at risk: the final optimizer does not read the program, it proves things about it, and anything it can prove away it removes. The standard for this part is the one set in the landscape lesson: judge each transform on the final artifact, not on the pass output.
The recipe, instantiated for bcfl

items: Register the branch in `lib/Plugin.cpp`: `Name == "minishield-bcfl"` → `FPM.addPass(minishield::BogusControlFlowPass())`, next to `minishield-flatten` and `minishield-stats`.

Write the guard `BcflEligibility::check(F)`: the function has at least one conditional branch; no `unreachable`, no `musttail`, no inline assembly — the shared negative fixtures in `tests/ir/` already cover those shapes. Rejection prints a named diagnostic and leaves the function untouched.
Write the builder: for each conditional branch, insert a gate block that evaluates an opaque predicate over a seed, with the original target on the true side and a new dead block on the false side.
Orchestrate in `BogusControlFlowPass::run` exactly like `FlatteningPass::run`: guard, build, verify.
Close with the fixture pair plus the differential: both modules verify, both binaries run identically.

blocks.text: The fixture is `grade`, a function with one conditional branch — three blocks at `-O0`. The opaque predicate is a product of two consecutive integers: given a seed `s`, compute `s² − s`, which is `s·(s−1)`, and test whether it is even. One of `s` and `s−1` is always even, so the product is always even, so the predicate is always true — but that is a number-theoretic fact about the seed, not something the optimizer is given.
The transformed module

source_filename = "bcfl_fixture.c"
target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare i32 @printf(ptr noundef, ...)

@.fmt = private unnamed_addr constant [16 x i8] c"grades sum: %d\0A\00"

; bcfl: 4 new blocks. Each side's real target is now reached through a gate
; guarded by an opaque predicate (product of consecutive integers is even).
; The seeds are constants chosen at transform time; the redundant blocks are dead.
define i32 @grade(i32 noundef %score) {
entry:
  %seed_pass = alloca i32, align 4
  %seed_fail = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 987654, ptr %seed_pass, align 4
  store i32 135791, ptr %seed_fail, align 4
  %cmp = icmp sge i32 %score, 60
  br i1 %cmp, label %gate_pass, label %gate_fail
gate_pass:
  %sp = load i32, ptr %seed_pass, align 4
  %t = mul i32 %sp, %sp
  %d = sub i32 %t, %sp
  %p = urem i32 %d, 2
  %g = icmp eq i32 %p, 0
  br i1 %g, label %pass, label %bogus_pass
pass:
  ret i32 1
bogus_pass:
  store i32 0, ptr %seed_pass, align 4
  br label %pass
gate_fail:
  %sf = load i32, ptr %seed_fail, align 4
  %t2 = mul i32 %sf, %sf
  %d2 = sub i32 %t2, %sf
  %p2 = urem i32 %d2, 2
  %g2 = icmp eq i32 %p2, 0
  br i1 %g2, label %fail, label %bogus_fail
fail:
  ret i32 0
bogus_fail:
  store i32 0, ptr %seed_fail, align 4
  br label %fail
}

define i32 @main() {
  %r1 = call i32 @grade(i32 70)
  %r2 = call i32 @grade(i32 30)
  %sum = add i32 %r1, %r2
  %p = call i32 @printf(ptr @.fmt, i32 %sum)
  ret i32 0
}

Read it against the original. Entry now stores two seeds — `987654` and `135791`, chosen at transform time — into allocas. The original branch no longer reaches its real targets: `br i1 %cmp` goes to `gate_pass` and `gate_fail`. Each gate loads its seed, computes `mul` → `sub` → `urem 2` → `icmp eq 0`, and branches: the true side (the only side that ever runs) reaches the unchanged `pass`/`fail` blocks; the false side goes to a new `bogus_pass`/`bogus_fail` block that stores to the seed and falls through to the real target. The function goes from 3 blocks to 7, and the module from 517 to 1444 bytes. The redundant blocks are dead by construction — the gate always takes the true edge — and that is the point: they exist to be read, not to be executed.
Differential proof at -O0

$ opt-23 -passes=verify -disable-output bcfl_before.ll
$ opt-23 -passes=verify -disable-output bcfl_after.ll
$ clang-23 -O0 bcfl_before.ll -o bcfl_before_bin
$ clang-23 -O0 bcfl_after.ll -o bcfl_after_bin
$ ./bcfl_before_bin
grades sum: 1
$ ./bcfl_after_bin
grades sum: 1
$ diff <(./bcfl_before_bin) <(./bcfl_after_bin)
(identical)

Both modules verify; both binaries print the same line — `grade(70)` returns 1, `grade(30)` returns 0, sum 1 either way. Note what is not evidence here: the `-O0` ELF size does not move (16624 bytes for both binaries), because section alignment swallows the difference — the module's byte count, 517 → 1444, is the honest measure of what the transform added.
What -O2 does to it

Now run the final optimizer over the obfuscated module. The seeds are constants, so the gate's arithmetic is a compile-time constant: the predicate folds to true, the false edges die, the redundant blocks (whose only instruction is a store to a seed nothing reads afterward) are eliminated, and the gates merge away. Seven blocks become one:

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare i32 @printf(ptr noundef, ...)

@.fmt = private unnamed_addr constant [16 x i8] c"grades sum: %d\0A\00"

; -O2 on the bcfl module: the seeds are constants, so the gate predicates
; fold, the dead blocks are removed, and the original branch linearizes.
define i32 @grade(i32 noundef %score) {
entry:
  %cmp = icmp sgt i32 %score, 59
  %. = zext i1 %cmp to i32
  ret i32 %.
}

define i32 @main() {
  %p = call i32 @printf(ptr @.fmt, i32 1)
  ret i32 0
}

`grade` is back to a single block — `icmp sgt i32 %score, 59` (the optimizer's own rewrite of `score >= 60`), a `zext`, a `ret` — and `main` has folded the two `grade` calls into the constant `1`. The transform is entirely gone. Keep two mechanisms separate. First, the constant seed: the predicate *computes* to a constant, so everything above it folds. Second, what happens when the seed is not a constant — replace both stores with `store i32 %score`: the predicate is now over runtime data, and the optimizer still does not dissolve the gate by proving it. A minimal probe (a bare branch on `s·(s−1) % 2 == 0` over an argument) shows LLVM 23's `-O2` normalizing the predicate to `x·(x−1)` with `and 1` and turning the branch into a `select` — but keeping it: the evenness of a product of consecutive integers is not proven in this context. The runtime-seed module dissolves anyway, 7 → 1 blocks, by a different route: the redundant blocks' stores are dead (nothing reads the seeds after the gates), DCE empties the blocks, and the empty fallthroughs merge. The predicate was never proven; the structure was simply emptied.

The one content the optimizer cannot delete is a side effect. Put an opaque call in each redundant block (`call void @record_trace(i32 7)` and `(i32 9)`) and the dead blocks no longer empty: the calls must be kept. `-O2`'s answer is to merge the two dead blocks into a single sink on the false side of a still-live gate branch — `br i1 %g, label %common.ret, label %common.ret.sink.split` — with one hoisted call and a `select` choosing which argument to pass. Seven blocks become three; runtime behavior is still identical, because the predicate really is always true and the sink really is never executed. What survives of the transform is a hoisted call behind a live-looking branch, not the four added blocks the pass emitted.

items: Constant seed: the predicate computes to a constant; fold → dead-edge elimination → dead-block DCE → merge. 7 blocks → 1.
Runtime seed, no side effect: the redundant blocks' stores are eliminated, the blocks become empty fallthroughs, and block merging removes the gates. 7 blocks → 1. The predicate is never proven.
Runtime seed + opaque call: the call must survive; both dead blocks merge into one sink on the live gate's false side, with a selected argument. 7 blocks → 3.

blocks.text: The three routes share a law, and the law recurs in this part: obfuscation adds structure without behavior, and the optimizer's job is exactly to remove structure without behavior. Opaque side effects are the only content the optimizer may not delete, and even those get hoisted and shrunk. The pass output (1444 bytes, 7 blocks) and the final artifact (1 block) are different programs to read; the one that ships is the second.

Checkpoint: In the transformed module the gates are always taken one way, yet -O2 does not dissolve them by proving that. (a) State the predicate and why it is always true, and name the rewrite the optimizer applies to it without finishing the job. (b) The constant-seed build dissolves 7 → 1 blocks and the runtime-seed build dissolves 7 → 1 blocks. Name the different mechanism that dissolves each. (c) In the survivor variant, where does the `record_trace` call end up after -O2, and why is that placement the strongest form the transform can take?

items: (a) A product of two consecutive integers: the gate computes `s·(s−1) % 2 == 0`. One of `s` and `s−1` is even, so the product is always even, so the predicate is always true. `instcombine` rewrites `s² − s` to `s·(s−1)` and `urem 2` to `and 1` — it normalizes the predicate's shape but does not prove its truth in branch context.

(b) Constant seed: the predicate computes to the constant true, the false edge is eliminated, the redundant blocks (whose only store targets a dead seed) are DCE'd, and the gates merge away — the function linearizes. Runtime seed, no side effect: the optimizer never proves the predicate; DCE removes the redundant blocks' dead stores, the blocks become empty fallthroughs, and block merging removes the gates themselves.

(c) Into a single sink block on the false side of a still-live gate branch (`common.ret.sink.split`), hoisted out of both dead blocks, with a `select` choosing which argument (7 or 9) to pass. The call is an opaque side effect, so DCE cannot delete it; the two dead blocks merge into one shared sink, collapsing the obfuscated pair of calls to one — and because the gate's predicate really is always true, the sink never runs, so behavior stays identical.

lessons.title: String encryption
lessons.summary: OLLVM string encryption as a learner pass: the plaintext constant is replaced by an encrypted blob plus a key and a decrypt loop, the -O0 proof that the output is identical and `strings` finds nothing, and the -O2 proof that the decrypt loop over constants is itself a constant — the plaintext returns as immediates and the blobs are deleted.
lessons.takeaway: String encryption moves the literals out of `.rodata` and behind a runtime XOR, so a static reader of the artifact sees only blobs. Like every transform in this part, its worth is a property of the final artifact: at -O2 the loop constant-folds, the plaintext returns as immediate values, and the encryption exists only at the optimization level where the loop cannot be folded.

blocks.text: The first move in any static reading of a binary is its strings: the URLs, keys, magic words, and format literals the program uses. OLLVM's string encryption attacks exactly that: each plaintext constant becomes an encrypted blob plus a per-byte key, and each use becomes a decrypt loop that reconstructs the plaintext into a stack buffer at runtime. The program still computes the plaintext — the transform changes where the bytes sit, not what they are.

As a MiniShield pass this follows the same five seams as the previous lesson: `minishield-strenc` in the registry; a guard for functions whose string constants are reachable (no `musttail`, no inline assembly, the shared `tests/ir/` fixtures); a builder that replaces each `c"..."` global with an `@enc`/`@key` pair and inserts a per-byte XOR loop at the use; the same orchestration; and the fixture pair below, differentially verified.
The transformed module
The fixture is `banner`, which `puts` the constant `"minishield\0"` — one global, one call, a 305-byte module. After the transform:

source_filename = "strenc_fixture.c"
target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare i32 @puts(ptr noundef)

; The plaintext is out of the module: only the encrypted blob and the key remain.
@enc = private unnamed_addr constant [11 x i8] c"\37\76\ad\e2\04\6c\b7\f4\47\94\68"
@key = private unnamed_addr constant [11 x i8] c"\5a\1f\c3\8b\77\04\de\91\2b\f0\68"

define void @banner() {
entry:
  %buf = alloca [11 x i8], align 1
  %i = alloca i64, align 8
  store i64 0, ptr %i, align 8
  br label %loop
loop:
  %iv = load i64, ptr %i, align 8
  %c = icmp slt i64 %iv, 11
  br i1 %c, label %body, label %after
body:
  %gep_e = getelementptr inbounds [11 x i8], ptr @enc, i64 0, i64 %iv
  %e = load i8, ptr %gep_e
  %gep_k = getelementptr inbounds [11 x i8], ptr @key, i64 0, i64 %iv
  %k = load i8, ptr %gep_k
  %x = xor i8 %e, %k
  %gep_b = getelementptr inbounds [11 x i8], ptr %buf, i64 0, i64 %iv
  store i8 %x, ptr %gep_b
  %inc = add i64 %iv, 1
  store i64 %inc, ptr %i, align 8
  br label %loop
after:
  %b0 = getelementptr inbounds [11 x i8], ptr %buf, i64 0, i64 0
  %p = call i32 @puts(ptr %b0)
  ret void
}

define i32 @main() {
  call void @banner()
  ret i32 0
}

`@.str` is gone. In its place: `@enc`, the ciphertext, and `@key`, the per-byte key, both chosen at transform time — byte `i` of the plaintext is `@enc[i] xor @key[i]`, and the last byte is the encrypted NUL terminator (`0x00 xor 0x68`). `banner` allocates a stack buffer and runs an `i64`-indexed loop: load a ciphertext byte, load a key byte, XOR, store. The index is `i64` because `getelementptr` into an array takes `i64` indices — widening a 32-bit counter is the detail that breaks a hand-written version, which `opt` rejects with `expected 'i64'`. The plaintext now exists at runtime only in `%buf`, between the loop's exit and the `puts` call.
Differential proof

$ opt-23 -passes=verify -disable-output strenc_before.ll
$ opt-23 -passes=verify -disable-output strenc_after.ll
$ clang-23 -O0 strenc_before.ll -o strenc_before_bin
$ clang-23 -O0 strenc_after.ll -o strenc_after_bin
$ diff <(./strenc_before_bin) <(./strenc_after_bin)
(identical)
$ strings strenc_before_bin | grep -x minishield
minishield
$ strings strenc_after_bin | grep -x minishield
(no match — exit status 1)

Two annotations. First, why `grep -x`: binaries built under the conda toolchain carry the toolchain's own path in their note sections — `/home/.../minishield/...` — so a bare `grep minishield` hits that path noise in *both* binaries. `-x` anchors on the whole line, so only a real string line matches. Second, the cost: the module grows from 305 to 1175 bytes to move an 11-byte literal behind a loop.
What -O2 does to it

target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare i32 @puts(ptr noundef)

; -O2 on the strenc module: the decrypt loop over constants is itself
; a constant. The result is emitted as immediates; @enc and @key are gone.
define void @banner() {
entry:
  %buf = alloca [11 x i8], align 8
  store <8 x i8> <i8 109, i8 105, i8 110, i8 105, i8 115, i8 104, i8 105, i8 101>, ptr %buf, align 8
  %gep_b.8 = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %buf, i64 8
  store i8 108, ptr %gep_b.8, align 8
  %gep_b.9 = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %buf, i64 9
  store i8 100, ptr %gep_b.9, align 1
  %gep_b.10 = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %buf, i64 10
  store i8 0, ptr %gep_b.10, align 2
  %p = call i32 @puts(ptr nonnull dereferenceable(1) %buf)
  ret void
}

define noundef i32 @main() {
  %buf.i = alloca [11 x i8], align 8
  call void @llvm.lifetime.start.p0(ptr nonnull %buf.i)
  store <8 x i8> <i8 109, i8 105, i8 110, i8 105, i8 115, i8 104, i8 105, i8 101>, ptr %buf.i, align 8
  %gep_b.8.i = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %buf.i, i64 8
  store i8 108, ptr %gep_b.8.i, align 8
  %gep_b.9.i = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %buf.i, i64 9
  store i8 100, ptr %gep_b.9.i, align 1
  %gep_b.10.i = getelementptr inbounds nuw i8, ptr %buf.i, i64 10
  store i8 0, ptr %gep_b.10.i, align 2
  %p.i = call i32 @puts(ptr nonnull dereferenceable(1) %buf.i)
  call void @llvm.lifetime.end.p0(ptr nonnull %buf.i)
  ret i32 0
}

The decrypt loop's operands are two constant arrays, so the whole loop is a compile-time constant. `-O2` replaces it with immediate stores — `store <8 x i8> <i8 109, i8 105, i8 110, i8 105, i8 115, i8 104, i8 105, i8 101>` is `minishie`, plus `l`, `d`, and NUL as separate stores — and deletes `@enc` and `@key` entirely. The trap is in the test: `grep minishield` on the -O2 module finds nothing, so a reader who probes the artifact with the same `strings`-style check concludes the plaintext is still hidden. It is not: it is back, as immediate values in the stores, not as a string literal — a disassembler reading the store's immediates sees the bytes directly. The property the transform provided was never “the optimizer cannot reconstruct the plaintext”; it was “the plaintext is not a contiguous literal in the artifact at the shipped optimization level.”

items: Before the transform, any level: the literal sits in `.rodata`; `strings` finds it.
After the transform, -O0: blob + key + runtime loop; `strings` finds nothing; the cost is a stack buffer and a byte loop at every call.

After the transform, -O2: the loop constant-folds to immediates, the globals are deleted, and the bytes are visible in the disassembly's immediate fields. The artifact is no harder to read than the unencrypted one.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: (a) In the transformed module, where does the plaintext exist at runtime, and which two globals hold its material? (b) `strings` on the -O0 binary finds nothing, and `grep minishield` on the -O2 module finds nothing. What actually returns at -O2, in what form, and why does that make the -O0 `strings` test a misleading probe of the final artifact? (c) State the condition on the final pipeline under which string encryption's property actually holds in a shipped binary.

items: (a) In a stack buffer (`%buf`), reconstructed byte by byte by the XOR loop and present only between the loop's exit and the `puts` call. Its material lives in two globals, `@enc` (the ciphertext) and `@key` (the per-byte key); the plaintext itself is present in no global.

(b) At -O2 the decrypt loop over two constant arrays is constant-folded: the plaintext returns as immediate values (`store <8 x i8> <i8 109, ...>`), not as a string literal — so `grep minishield` finds nothing even though a disassembler reading the stores sees the bytes. The -O0 `strings` test measured “no contiguous literal in this -O0 binary”; it says nothing about the final artifact, where the same transform is folded back into plain stores.

(c) The transform must be the last step of the pipeline — applied after the final optimization, so that no later optimizer pass (a second `opt -O2`, LTO at link) can fold the decrypt loop. That is the deployment rule the part closes with in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Subroutine splitting
lessons.summary: OLLVM subroutine splitting as a learner pass: each non-entry block becomes an internal subroutine, the original function becomes a state dispatcher, the differential proof that behavior is unchanged, and the -O2 proof that the inliner is the transform's exact inverse — every part inlines back and the recovered loop is vectorized.
lessons.takeaway: Subroutine splitting is a pure structural decomposition: the CFG's blocks become module-level internal functions driven by a state switch. It is the most fragile of the three transforms, because it adds no predicate, no data, and no side effect — only a decomposition, and the optimizer's inliner reconstructs it exactly.

blocks.text: Subroutine splitting (OLLVM's `subdiv`) takes a function with a tangled CFG and moves each of its non-entry blocks into its own `internal` function. The original keeps its entry and becomes a dispatcher over a state variable: a `switch` that calls the right part and loops back. Each part looks like an unrelated helper, and the shape of the CFG — the thing static analysis keys on — is no longer visible inside any single function.

The five seams again, with the pattern from the previous lesson: `minishield-subdivide` in the registry; a guard for functions whose blocks are movable (no PHI nodes whose incoming edges would need a home in the split — the fixture below is PHI-free at -O0, with all state in allocas; no `musttail`, no inline assembly); a builder that cuts each non-entry block into an `internal` function taking the needed allocas as pointer arguments, converts each conditional branch into a `select` that writes the next state, converts each unconditional branch into a constant store, and turns `ret` into the part's return; the same orchestration; and the fixture pair, differentially verified.
The transformed module

The fixture is `total`, a loop accumulating `a·b`, in its -O0 shape: five blocks (`entry`, `cond`, `body`, `inc`, `exit`), four allocas, no PHIs. After the transform — 2 → 6 functions, module 1123 → 2232 bytes:

source_filename = "subdivide_fixture.c"
target triple = "x86_64-conda-linux-gnu"

declare i32 @printf(ptr noundef, ...)

@.fmt = private unnamed_addr constant [15 x i8] c"total(6,4)=%d\0A\00"

; subdivide: each non-entry block becomes an internal subroutine. The original
; function keeps only the entry setup and becomes the state dispatcher.
; State numbering follows block order: 1=cond, 2=body, 3=inc, 4=exit.

define internal void @total.1(ptr %p_i, ptr %p_b, ptr %p_state) {
  %i = load i32, ptr %p_i, align 4
  %b2 = load i32, ptr %p_b, align 4
  %c = icmp slt i32 %i, %b2
  %ns = select i1 %c, i32 2, i32 4
  store i32 %ns, ptr %p_state, align 4
  ret void
}

define internal void @total.2(ptr %p_a, ptr %p_sum, ptr %p_state) {
  %a2 = load i32, ptr %p_a, align 4
  %s = load i32, ptr %p_sum, align 4
  %ns = add nsw i32 %s, %a2
  store i32 %ns, ptr %p_sum, align 4
  store i32 3, ptr %p_state, align 4
  ret void
}

define internal void @total.3(ptr %p_i, ptr %p_state) {
  %i2 = load i32, ptr %p_i, align 4
  %inc2 = add nsw i32 %i2, 1
  store i32 %inc2, ptr %p_i, align 4
  store i32 1, ptr %p_state, align 4
  ret void
}

define internal i32 @total.4(ptr %p_sum) {
  %r = load i32, ptr %p_sum, align 4
  ret i32 %r
}

define i32 @total(i32 noundef %a, i32 noundef %b) {
entry:
  %p_a = alloca i32, align 4
  %p_b = alloca i32, align 4
  %p_sum = alloca i32, align 4
  %p_i = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 %a, ptr %p_a, align 4
  store i32 %b, ptr %p_b, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %p_sum, align 4
  store i32 0, ptr %p_i, align 4
  %p_state = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 1, ptr %p_state, align 4
  br label %dispatch
dispatch:
  %s = load i32, ptr %p_state, align 4
  switch i32 %s, label %invalid [
    i32 1, label %c1
    i32 2, label %c2
    i32 3, label %c3
    i32 4, label %c4
  ]
c1:
  call void @total.1(ptr %p_i, ptr %p_b, ptr %p_state)
  br label %dispatch
c2:
  call void @total.2(ptr %p_a, ptr %p_sum, ptr %p_state)
  br label %dispatch
c3:
  call void @total.3(ptr %p_i, ptr %p_state)
  br label %dispatch
c4:
  %r = call i32 @total.4(ptr %p_sum)
  ret i32 %r
invalid:
  unreachable
}

define i32 @main() {
  %r = call i32 @total(i32 6, i32 4)
  %p = call i32 @printf(ptr @.fmt, i32 %r)
  ret i32 0
}

Read the parts first. `total.1` is the old `cond` block: it computes the branch decision, but instead of branching it writes the next state — `%ns = select i1 %c, i32 2, i32 4`: loop again (state 2) or exit (state 4). `total.2` is `body` (accumulate, then write state 3). `total.3` is `inc` (increment, then write state 1, back to the condition). `total.4` is `exit` — the only part that returns a value, the accumulated sum. The conditional branch became a state assignment; the unconditional branch became a constant store; `ret` became the part's return. Now the dispatcher: `total` keeps its entry setup, adds a `%p_state` alloca initialized to 1, and loops over `switch i32 %s`: each case calls the matching part and returns to the dispatch; case 4 returns the part's value; the `invalid` default is `unreachable`, because the state is only ever assigned 1 through 4.
Differential proof

$ opt-23 -passes=verify -disable-output subdivide_before.ll
$ opt-23 -passes=verify -disable-output subdivide_after.ll
$ clang-23 -O0 subdivide_before.ll -o subdivide_before_bin
$ clang-23 -O0 subdivide_after.ll -o subdivide_after_bin
$ diff <(./subdivide_before_bin) <(./subdivide_after_bin)
(identical)
$ ./subdivide_after_bin
total(6,4)=24
$ grep -c '^define' subdivide_before.ll
2
$ grep -c '^define' subdivide_after.ll
6

Both modules verify; both binaries print `total(6,4)=24`; the module gains four `internal` functions. The -O0 binary sizes barely move (16624 vs 16632 bytes) — alignment again — so the honest measures are the function count and the module bytes.
What -O2 does to it

Every `total.N` is `internal` (no definition outside the module can reference it) and has exactly one caller — the dispatcher. That is the inliner's exact target, and -O2 inlines all four parts, recovers the original loop, and then optimizes the recovered loop. The fragment below is the `total` function from the -O2 module (the attribute groups and loop metadata it references sit at the end of the module):

define i32 @total(i32 noundef %a, i32 noundef %b) local_unnamed_addr #1 {
dispatch.outer4:
  %c.i.jt129 = icmp sgt i32 %b, 0
  br i1 %c.i.jt129, label %dispatch.outer4.jt3.lr.ph, label %c4

dispatch.outer4.jt3.lr.ph:                        ; preds = %dispatch.outer4
  %min.iters.check = icmp ult i32 %b, 8
  br i1 %min.iters.check, label %dispatch.outer4.jt3.preheader, label %vector.ph

vector.ph:                                        ; preds = %dispatch.outer4.jt3.lr.ph
  %n.vec = and i32 %b, 2147483640
  %broadcast.splatinsert = insertelement <4 x i32> poison, i32 %a, i64 0
  %broadcast.splat = shufflevector <4 x i32> %broadcast.splatinsert, <4 x i32> poison, <4 x i32> zeroinitializer
  br label %vector.body

vector.body:                                      ; preds = %vector.body, %vector.ph
  %index = phi i32 [ 0, %vector.ph ], [ %index.next, %vector.body ]
  %vec.phi = phi <4 x i32> [ zeroinitializer, %vector.ph ], [ %0, %vector.body ]
  %vec.phi32 = phi <4 x i32> [ zeroinitializer, %vector.ph ], [ %1, %vector.body ]
  %0 = add <4 x i32> %vec.phi, %broadcast.splat
  %1 = add <4 x i32> %vec.phi32, %broadcast.splat
  %index.next = add nuw i32 %index, 8
  %2 = icmp eq i32 %index.next, %n.vec
  br i1 %2, label %middle.block, label %vector.body, !llvm.loop !0

middle.block:                                     ; preds = %vector.body
  %bin.rdx = add <4 x i32> %1, %0
  %3 = tail call i32 @llvm.vector.reduce.add.v4i32(<4 x i32> %bin.rdx)
  %cmp.n = icmp eq i32 %b, %n.vec
  br i1 %cmp.n, label %c4, label %dispatch.outer4.jt3.preheader

dispatch.outer4.jt3.preheader:                    ; preds = %dispatch.outer4.jt3.lr.ph, %middle.block
  %p_sum.0.ph2031.ph = phi i32 [ 0, %dispatch.outer4.jt3.lr.ph ], [ %3, %middle.block ]
  %inc2.i.sink30.ph = phi i32 [ 0, %dispatch.outer4.jt3.lr.ph ], [ %n.vec, %middle.block ]
  br label %dispatch.outer4.jt3

dispatch.outer4.jt3:                              ; preds = %dispatch.outer4.jt3.preheader, %dispatch.outer4.jt3
  %p_sum.0.ph2031 = phi i32 [ %ns.i1, %dispatch.outer4.jt3 ], [ %p_sum.0.ph2031.ph, %dispatch.outer4.jt3.preheader ]
  %inc2.i.sink30 = phi i32 [ %inc2.i, %dispatch.outer4.jt3 ], [ %inc2.i.sink30.ph, %dispatch.outer4.jt3.preheader ]
  %ns.i1 = add nsw i32 %p_sum.0.ph2031, %a
  %inc2.i = add nuw nsw i32 %inc2.i.sink30, 1
  %c.i.jt1 = icmp slt i32 %inc2.i, %b
  br i1 %c.i.jt1, label %dispatch.outer4.jt3, label %c4, !llvm.loop !3

c4:                                               ; preds = %dispatch.outer4.jt3, %middle.block, %dispatch.outer4
  %p_sum.0.ph20.lcssa = phi i32 [ 0, %dispatch.outer4 ], [ %3, %middle.block ], [ %ns.i1, %dispatch.outer4.jt3 ]
  ret i32 %p_sum.0.ph20.lcssa
}

Note what the optimizer did to the recovered loop: it did not stop at the original — it vectorized it, four additions wide, closing each vector iteration with `llvm.vector.reduce.add.v4i32`. The contrast with the unobfuscated original is the point: `-O2` on the *plain* module strength-reduces the same loop to the closed form `mul i32 %b, %a` plus a select, while `-O2` on the *obfuscated* module recovers the loop and vectorizes it. Both end states compute `a·b`; they are different programs, because the inlined state machine changed how the optimizer saw the loop. The transform itself — six functions, a switch, a state machine — is gone, along with the 2232 bytes.

rows: 1 block — seed fold, or dead-block DCE + merge

blocks.text: Subdivide is the most fragile of the three, and the reason is now visible: it adds structure without content. Bogus control flow adds a predicate the optimizer cannot prove (and, with an opaque side effect, content the optimizer may not delete); string encryption moves data behind a loop that at least must be executed at -O0. Subdivide adds nothing but a decomposition of what was already there — and a decomposition is exactly what the inliner removes. A transform whose output is inlining fuel cannot survive an optimizer that inlines.

Checkpoint: (a) In the transformed module, how does the original's conditional branch appear inside the parts, and what is the role of the dispatcher's `invalid` case? (b) Name the two properties of the `total.N` functions that make them guaranteed inlining targets at -O2. (c) Why is subroutine splitting the most fragile of the three OLLVM transforms in this part?

items: (a) As a `select` that writes the next state into the shared state slot: `total.1` ends with `%ns = select i1 %c, i32 2, i32 4; store i32 %ns, ptr %p_state`, and the dispatcher's `switch` re-branches on the stored value. The `invalid` case is the `switch`'s default and is `unreachable`: the state is only ever assigned 1 through 4, so the default encodes the state machine's invariant as dead code.

(b) `internal` linkage — no definition outside the module can reference them — and a single caller, the dispatcher. The inliner can see the entire callee and its only use, so both the call and the function disappear.

(c) It adds structure without content: no new predicate, no moved data, no side effect — only a decomposition of the existing CFG. The inliner, its exact inverse, undoes the decomposition and then optimizes the recovered loop (here, vectorizing it four-wide). The other two transforms leave something the optimizer cannot simply delete: an unprovable predicate behind a live branch, or bytes behind a loop.

lessons.title: What the final optimizer keeps
lessons.summary: The deployment rule that makes OLLVM-style obfuscation survive: the transform must run after the final optimization. Proven with the learner's real plugin — flattening clang -O2's output keeps the dispatcher and runs identically, re-running -O2 on the artifact removes the dispatcher, and two pipeline traps (a pass named `O2` does not exist; `optnone` makes optional passes skip silently) decide which inputs the rule can apply to at all.
lessons.takeaway: Obfuscation is a pipeline position, not just a pass: apply it last, to the final optimized IR, or the next optimizer pass gets a second look at the artifact and erases it. The proof is the learner's own plugin on a real -O2 module — and the negative proof is one more -O2 over the obfuscated artifact, which removes the dispatcher entirely.

blocks.text: Lessons 83 through 85 each ended the same way: -O2 over the pass output dissolved the transform. The dissolution was not a defect of the transforms; it was the pipeline order — in every case the transform ran on unoptimized IR, and the final optimizer then ran over it. The deployment rule this lesson proves: obfuscation must be the last transform, applied to the final optimized artifact. The proof uses the plugin the learner has been building — the flattening pass from Volume 2, `build/libMiniShield.so` — not a reference implementation.
A function that survives -O2
The fixture is `classify`, a branched function over a runtime input:

Why not reuse `total` from the previous lesson? Because -O2 strength-reduces it to `a·b` before any obfuscation runs: the five-block loop is gone, and there is nothing left to transform. `classify`'s branches depend on a runtime input the optimizer cannot fold, and the call is `noinline`, so the function keeps its shape through the final optimization. At -O2 it is five blocks — labels `3`, `5`, `7`, `9`, `12`, the numeric labels clang gives -O2 IR — with a PHI at the join:

define dso_local range(i32 0, -2147483648) i32 @classify(i32 noundef %0) local_unnamed_addr #0 {
  %2 = icmp slt i32 %0, 0
  br i1 %2, label %3, label %5

3:                                                ; preds = %1
  %4 = sub nsw i32 100, %0
  br label %12

5:                                                ; preds = %1
  %6 = icmp samesign ult i32 %0, 50
  br i1 %6, label %7, label %9

7:                                                ; preds = %5
  %8 = shl nuw nsw i32 %0, 1
  br label %12

9:                                                ; preds = %5
  %10 = lshr i32 %0, 1
  %11 = add nuw nsw i32 %10, 5
  br label %12

12:                                               ; preds = %9, %7, %3
  %13 = phi i32 [ %4, %3 ], [ %8, %7 ], [ %11, %9 ]
  ret i32 %13
}
Flatten after -O2, with the real plugin

$ clang-23 -O2 -S -emit-llvm persist_fixture.c -o persist_o2.ll
$ opt-23 -load-pass-plugin=build/libMiniShield.so \
    -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
    -S persist_o2.ll -o persist_final.ll
[MiniShield] eligible: classify
Number of Phis: 1
[MiniShield] rejected: main: intrinsic calls are outside this prototype's scope

Three lines, all correct: `classify` is eligible, the pass counts its one PHI (the join block's, which the preparation stage demotes — visible in the artifact below), and `main` is rejected by the learner's own guard: at -O2 it still carries `llvm.lifetime.start`/`llvm.lifetime.end` intrinsic calls, which the support contract established in Volume 2 excludes — the guard prints its named reason and leaves the function untouched. The pipeline is two stages: the final optimizer first (`-O2` to a `.ll`), then the obfuscation (`function(minishield-flatten)`), then `verify`.
The artifact

define dso_local range(i32 0, -2147483648) i32 @classify(i32 noundef %0) local_unnamed_addr #0 {
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  %.reg2mem = alloca i32, align 4
  %2 = icmp slt i32 %0, 0
  br i1 %2, label %3, label %5

3:                                                ; preds = %ms.dispatch, %1
  %4 = sub nsw i32 100, %0
  store i32 %4, ptr %.reg2mem, align 4
  br label %12

5:                                                ; preds = %ms.dispatch, %1
  %6 = icmp samesign ult i32 %0, 50
  br i1 %6, label %7, label %9

7:                                                ; preds = %ms.dispatch, %5
  %8 = shl nuw nsw i32 %0, 1
  store i32 %8, ptr %.reg2mem, align 4
  br label %12

9:                                                ; preds = %ms.dispatch, %5
  %10 = lshr i32 %0, 1
  %11 = add nuw nsw i32 %10, 5
  store i32 %11, ptr %.reg2mem, align 4
  br label %12

12:                                               ; preds = %ms.dispatch, %9, %7, %3
  %.reload = load i32, ptr %.reg2mem, align 4
  ret i32 %.reload

ms.dispatch:                                      ; No predecessors!
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %3
    i32 1, label %5
    i32 2, label %7
    i32 3, label %9
    i32 4, label %12
  ]

ms.invalid:                                       ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  unreachable
}

This is the learner's flattening output on -O2's IR, and it is worth reading block by block. First the preparation: the values the optimized blocks share have moved to the stack — the `phi` at join block `12` (which picked among the three branch results) is gone, replaced by a `%.reg2mem` slot each producing branch stores into and the join loads from — while the optimized blocks themselves are intact, including the `shl nuw nsw` where -O2 wrote the `x * 2`. Demoting PHIs and escaping values preserves behavior by itself. Then the state machine: an `ms.state` slot, an `ms.dispatch` block whose `switch` over `ms.current` maps the five states onto the five optimized blocks, and `ms.invalid` → `unreachable` as the switch's default. The transform lays the scaffolding on top of the optimized function; whether the scaffolding is wired to the entry is a separate question, and the artifact answers it plainly.
The entry the pass does — and does not — rewire

`ms.dispatch` carries the `; No predecessors!` comment: in this build the entry's conditional branch is not yet rewired — `entry` still reaches `3` and `5` directly, so the dispatcher is scaffolding that has been added but not connected. The build is not idle, though: it does rewire an unconditional entry. The fixture below is the Volume 2 exit-evidence shape — an unconditional jump into a loop header with a PHI — written by hand rather than produced by clang, because `clang -O0` marks every function `optnone` and the optional pass skips `optnone` functions silently (the second of this lesson's pipeline traps), and it carries a second function with a conditional entry, so one module shows both cases:

$ opt-23 -passes=verify -disable-output wire_fixture.ll
$ opt-23 -load-pass-plugin=build/libMiniShield.so \
    -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
    -S wire_fixture.ll -o wire_flat.ll
[MiniShield] eligible: count_to
Number of Phis: 1
[MiniShield] eligible: main
Number of Phis: 0
$ grep -A1 'store i32 0, ptr %ms.state' wire_flat.ll
  store i32 0, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %ms.dispatch
$ grep '^ms.dispatch:' wire_flat.ll
ms.dispatch:                                      ; preds = %entry
ms.dispatch:                                      ; No predecessors!
$ clang-23 wire_fixture.ll -o wire_orig
$ clang-23 wire_flat.ll -o wire_flat_bin
$ echo 5 | ./wire_orig  &&  echo 5 | ./wire_flat_bin
count_to(5)=5
count_to(5)=5

In `count_to` the entry's branch is replaced by a store of the successor's state (`0`, the id of the first block) and a jump to the dispatcher, and its `ms.dispatch` now has a real predecessor. In `main` — as in `classify` — the entry's conditional branch is untouched, and its `ms.dispatch` has none. The conditional-entry case is what the CondBr lesson builds: every original terminator stores its destination state and jumps to the dispatcher, which is what the Volume 2 exit evidence's fully wired listing shows. The persistence rule does not depend on that gap: the artifact is exactly what the final optimizer sees, and the control below measures what the final optimizer does to it.
Behavior identity

$ clang-23 persist_final.ll -o persist_final_bin
$ clang-23 -O2 persist_fixture.c -o persist_orig_bin
$ echo 42 | ./persist_final_bin  &&  echo 42 | ./persist_orig_bin
classify(42)=84
classify(42)=84
$ echo 7 | ./persist_final_bin  &&  echo 7 | ./persist_orig_bin
classify(7)=14
classify(7)=14
$ echo -7 | ./persist_final_bin  &&  echo -7 | ./persist_orig_bin
classify(-7)=107
classify(-7)=107

Three inputs, one per branch: negative (`-7 → 100 − (−7) = 107`), mid (`7 → 2·7 = 14`), high (`42 → 42/2 + 5 = 84`). The obfuscated artifact and the plain -O2 binary agree on all three: the flattened -O2 function is a correct program.
The control: re-run -O2

$ grep -c 'switch i32' persist_final.ll
1
$ opt-23 -O2 -S persist_final.ll -o persist_reopt.ll
$ grep -c 'switch i32' persist_reopt.ll
0

One more pass of -O2 over the obfuscated artifact and the dispatcher is gone: the `switch` count goes 1 → 0, `ms.state` and `ms.dispatch` are deleted, and `classify` is back to plain branches. Behavior is unchanged — the re-optimized binary still prints the same three lines — but the artifact is structurally unobfuscated again. An artifact is only as obfuscated as the last transform that ran on it; a transform that runs before the final optimizer hands the optimizer a second look, and the optimizer takes it.
Two pipeline traps

items: `O2` is not a pass name. `opt -passes='O2,function(minishield-flatten)'` fails with `unknown pass name 'O2'`: optimization levels are not elements of a pass pipeline. The level inside a pipeline is spelled `default<O2>` (the default O2 pipeline), and `default<O2>,function(minishield-flatten)` parses — the spelling matters when you want the whole rule in one command.

`optnone` makes optional passes skip silently. `clang -O0` marks every function `optnone` (three in this fixture's -O0 module; zero in the -O2 module). `minishield-flatten` is an optional pass — registered through the pipeline-parsing callback, not required by the pipeline's shape — and optional passes skip `optnone` functions without a diagnostic: running it on the -O0 IR changes nothing and prints zero `[MiniShield]` lines. Nor does `default<O2>` rescue it: -O2 respects `optnone` and leaves the attribute in place, so the one-shot `default<O2>,function(minishield-flatten)` on -O0 IR also flattens nothing. The rule's input must be real final-optimization IR, not a -O0 draft.

blocks.text: Four lessons, one law. The three transforms add structure — gates, blobs, decompositions — and the final optimizer removes structure; each -O2 section showed the removal from the transform's side (constant folding, dead-store elimination, inlining), and this lesson shows the rule from the deployment side: the transform must be last in the pipeline that produces the shipped binary. “Last” is a position, not a property: the control proves that one more optimizer pass after the transform erases it, so an obfuscated IR that is later re-optimized — by a second `opt`, by LTO at link, by a downstream tool — is not an obfuscated artifact. The question every hardening claim in this part must answer is the one from the landscape lesson: what does the final artifact look like?

Checkpoint: (a) Why does the persistence demo use `classify` instead of the previous lesson's `total`? (b) The flatten pass on the -O0 IR prints no diagnostics and changes nothing. Name the attribute responsible, and the class of pass whose behavior it controls. (c) State the deployment rule in one sentence, and say what the re-optimization control (switch count 1 → 0) proves about an artifact that is obfuscated and then optimized again.

items: (a) Because -O2 strength-reduces `total` to the closed form `a·b` (a `mul` plus a select) before any obfuscation runs: the five-block loop is gone and there is nothing left to transform. `classify`'s branches depend on a runtime input the optimizer cannot fold, and the call is `noinline`, so it keeps its five-block structure through the final optimization.

(b) `optnone`, which `clang -O0` attaches to every function. It controls optional passes — passes added through the pipeline-parsing callback (like `minishield-flatten`) rather than required by the pipeline's shape: an optional pass skips `optnone` functions entirely, with no diagnostic.

(c) Obfuscation must be the last transform in the pipeline that produces the shipped binary, applied to the final optimized IR. The control proves the negative: one more -O2 over the obfuscated artifact removes the dispatcher's `switch` (1 → 0) and the function is back to plain branches — behavior unchanged, structure unobfuscated. “Last” means nothing after it; an artifact that is re-optimized after obfuscation is not an obfuscated artifact.

lessons.title: Position independence
lessons.summary: Read PIE, ASLR, and RELRO the way the toolchain actually implements them: zero trace in the IR (the -pie and -no-pie modules are byte-identical), everything in the ELF (EXEC vs DYN, FLAGS_1 PIE, absolute vs load-base-relative relocations, the RELRO segment), and the runtime proof — the fixed-address build prints the same pointers on every run, the PIE build prints a new base on every run.
lessons.takeaway: Position independence is hardening that lives in the linker and the loader, not the IR: the position model leaves no mark in the module, the decision is recorded in the ELF header and the relocation table, ASLR randomizes the load base, and full RELRO closes the last writable GOT by moving .got.plt inside the read-only segment. A pass plugin can express none of it — it is a build-flag and load-time decision, verified with readelf, not opt.

blocks.text: The first three parts of this volume left traces you can read: CFI left checks in the IR (`llvm.type.test` + `llvm.ubsantrap`), the canary left an attribute in the IR (`sspstrong`), the OLLVM transforms changed the IR's structure. This chapter asks where position independence lives, and the answer is: not in the IR at all. The threat it answers is the predictable-layout row of the landscape's threat table: ASLR randomizes the stack, heap, and library bases, but an executable that is not position independent is mapped at its fixed file addresses on every run, so every address an attacker would need — a function, a GOT slot, a return target — is stable in advance. PIE makes the program itself a load-time value.
The IR says nothing
The fixture prints the address of a global and the address of `main` — the two kinds of self-address an attacker computes:

$ clang-23 -no-pie -O0 -S -emit-llvm pie_fixture.c -o pie_nopie.ll
clang-23: warning: argument unused during compilation: '-no-pie'
$ clang-23 -pie -O0 -S -emit-llvm pie_fixture.c -o pie_pie.ll
clang-23: warning: argument unused during compilation: '-pie'
$ cmp pie_nopie.ll pie_pie.ll
(identical — and again at -O2)

The two position models produce byte-identical modules — at `-O0` and at `-O2` — and the compiler even warns that the flag is unused on the IR path. Where the canary chapter found a hint in the IR that the backend acted on, here the IR carries nothing: an IR reader cannot tell the two builds apart, and an IR pass cannot express or detect the position model. The decision is made and recorded below the IR.
The executable says it

$ llvm-readelf-23 -h pie_nopie | grep Type
  Type:                              EXEC (Executable file)
$ llvm-readelf-23 -h pie_pie | grep Type
  Type:                              DYN (Shared object file)
$ llvm-readelf-23 -d pie_pie | grep FLAGS
  0x000000006ffffffb (FLAGS_1)      PIE

The `-no-pie` executable is `EXEC`: the loader maps it at the fixed addresses recorded in the file — the `0x201xxx` range the demo prints. The PIE executable is a `DYN`: a position-independent object the loader treats exactly like a shared library — it chooses a base, and every address in the image is computed from it. The `(FLAGS_1) PIE` tag in the dynamic section is the loader's marker. (This toolchain defaults to PIE — an unflagged build is `DYN` with the tag and randomized addresses — which is why every command below spells the flag out.)
The relocation table shows how "computed from the base" works:

$ llvm-objdump-23 -R pie_nopie
DYNAMIC RELOCATION RECORDS
OFFSET           TYPE                     VALUE
00000000002028a0 R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT        __libc_start_main
00000000002028a8 R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT        __gmon_start__
00000000002038e0 R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT       printf
$ llvm-objdump-23 -R pie_pie
DYNAMIC RELOCATION RECORDS
OFFSET           TYPE                     VALUE
00000000000027c0 R_X86_64_RELATIVE        *ABS*+0x16e0
00000000000027c8 R_X86_64_RELATIVE        *ABS*+0x1720
00000000000039b0 R_X86_64_RELATIVE        *ABS*+0x39b0
0000000000002980 R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT        __libc_start_main
...

The `-no-pie` executable's relocations are all library relocations: the loader writes the final addresses of the imported functions into its GOT slots. The PIE executable carries those same entries *plus* `R_X86_64_RELATIVE` records — `*ABS*+0x16e0` and so on — which the loader resolves as `load_base + offset`, filling the executable's own writable slots — here, the `.fini_array` and `.init_array` entries and a `.data` slot; the `.got` is not among them, its library slots still coming from the `GLOB_DAT` records both builds carry. The program's self-addresses are load-time values: `&global` is not a constant baked into the file, it is the randomized base plus an offset.
ASLR at runtime

$ for i in 1 2 3; do ./pie_nopie; done
global at 0x2038c0, main at 0x201680
global at 0x2038c0, main at 0x201680
global at 0x2038c0, main at 0x201680
$ for i in 1 2 3; do ./pie_pie; done
global at 0x603bc21939b8, main at 0x603bc2191730
global at 0x65386ac319b8, main at 0x65386ac2f730
global at 0x6072bb9f79b8, main at 0x6072bb9f5730

Three runs of the `-no-pie` build: identical addresses. The executable maps at its fixed file addresses on every run, on every machine, so an attacker who ships the binary ships every target address with it. Three runs of the PIE build: a new base each time, with the offset between `global` and `main` (`0x2288`) invariant — ASLR randomizes the base, not the layout.
